title: FAA Chief Demands $50 Billion After Flight Meltdown, But Democrats Push Back
snippet: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is demanding $50 billion in emergency FAA funding following a historic nationwide ground stop, but incoming Democratic leaders insist the agency already has billions in unspent money.
content:
WASHINGTON — Following a catastrophic nationwide flight shutdown that left travelers stranded across the country, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is dramatically escalating his demands for congressional funding, asking lawmakers for $50 billion to overhaul the Federal Aviation Administration's aging technology.

The staggering request comes just days after a historic air traffic control system failure on Friday grounded domestic flights nationwide. Duffy had originally sought $30 billion prior to the incident, but bumped his ask to $50 billion over the weekend, backed by a quick endorsement from President Donald Trump urging Congress to move "FAST!" on social media.

A Broken System and Big Bills

According to Duffy, Friday's crippling ground stop stemmed from an upgrade attempt in El Dorado, Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was transitioning an air traffic communication center from legacy copper wiring to modern fiber-optic lines. Whether the outage was triggered by faulty equipment or contractor error remains under investigation.

Appearing on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday, Duffy argued that the FAA's infrastructure is dangerously outdated, relying on software and towers built in the 1990s. "All I need is the money to finish it," Duffy said. "If they give me money today, I’ll be going tomorrow to build it."

Democrats Question Unspent Funds

However, Democrats—who are set to take the majority in Congress in January—are skeptical of the administration's sudden appeal. Lawmakers point out that a GOP-led spending bill passed last year already allocated $12.5 billion to the FAA, including $4.75 billion earmarked specifically for telecom modernization and system upgrades. Agency officials acknowledged Saturday that only about one-third of those modernization funds have been spent so far.

Reps. Rick Larsen and André Carson, the leading Democrats on House aviation panels, have demanded a formal briefing explaining why the administration needs tens of billions more while existing funds remain in the bank.

Other Democrats took aim at the administration's budget priorities, noting that billions of dollars have been directed toward immigration enforcement and Capitol construction projects rather than critical aviation infrastructure. Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth blasted the administration on social media, arguing that the White House has prioritized vanity projects over fixing the nation's air traffic control system.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, fired back even harder, characterizing Duffy’s $50 billion demand as "ransom" and asserting that "our air traffic controllers have been failed by Secretary Duffy."

The Path Forward in Congress

Despite the partisan crossfire, some key Democrats have left the door open for compromise. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen indicated he would support whatever funding is necessary to secure the nation's skies, though he insisted administration officials must come to Capitol Hill and properly justify the ask.

With a government funding deadline looming on December 11, outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson said Republicans intend to tackle FAA funding in an upcoming legislative package before their majority expires. Meanwhile, Missouri Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt is rallying support for his Modern Skies Act, a $30 billion proposal aimed at modernizing domestic air traffic control infrastructure.
